block-string.comment: A block literal. Its escapes still escape, so it is the ordinary string rule with a longer delimiter; it is listed before `string` so the opening `"""` is not claimed as an empty literal followed by a quote.
block-string.name: string.quoted.triple.kiln

raw-block-string.comment: Raw: nothing inside is interpreted, so the body has no patterns at all — which is exactly the difference the highlighting should show.
raw-block-string.name: string.quoted.triple.raw.kiln

interpolation.comment: A text literal carries `{expr}` holes — `"n is {f(a)}"` — and a hole holds a whole expression, so the language highlights inside it. `{{` and `}}` are the escaped single braces and are claimed first, before either can open a hole. The hole includes itself so the braces of a dict literal inside one balance rather than closing it. The raw literals above have no holes at all, which is the difference they exist to show.

number.comment: Hex and binary bit patterns first, so `0xFF` is one number rather than `0` followed by a name. `_` groups digits.

patterns.comment: The name being declared is highlighted as an entity, not as a plain identifier — it is what the outline and go-to-definition target.
`on click: handler` binds an event to a subroutine.

statement-word.comment: The statement words that lead a block or a check. Like the bitwise operators they are soft keywords in the language — a variable may still be named for one — which a grammar this size cannot tell apart, so a name that collides is highlighted as the keyword.
statement-word.name: keyword.control.kiln

expression-word.comment: The words that join or guard a value: `then` for the `if` written as a value, `otherwise` for what a failure or an absent optional falls back to, `check` for the call that returns early, `as` for the name `if some` binds, `in`/`to`/`step` for a range and the `for` that walks one, and `each`/`of`/`from` for `for each` and a list comprehension. Soft keywords too, with the same caveat as above.
expression-word.name: keyword.control.kiln

dot-call.comment: `raw.trim().uppercase()` — the dot-call sugar puts a command after `.`, so a called name there is a call, not a property. Listed before `member`, which would otherwise claim it.
dot-call.name: entity.name.function.call.kiln

member.comment: A name after `.` that is not called is a component property or event; `#dot-call` above claims the called ones.
member.name: variable.other.property.kiln

indirect.comment: `call through fp(...)` calls a function pointer. `through` means that only straight after `call` — it is a soft keyword and a variable may still be named for it — so the pair is matched together rather than the word alone.

bitwise.comment: The word operators — the bitwise ones, and `mod`. They are soft keywords in the language — a variable may be named for one — which a grammar this size cannot tell apart, so a name that collides is highlighted as the operator.
bitwise.name: keyword.operator.word.kiln

assignment.comment: A name on the left of `=` or of a compound `+=`/`-=`/`*=`/`/=`/`&=` is an assignment target or a form property, never a type — `text = "hi"` must not highlight as the `text` type.
